title: ABC Adventures
description: A playful literacy guide that helps young children recognize letters, sounds, and simple words through songs, objects, and confidence-building activities.
contentHtml:
ABC Adventures

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This child-friendly literacy guide helps young learners explore letters, sounds, pictures, and simple words in a fun, gentle way.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Recognize common alphabet letters.
  • Connect letters to sounds.
  • Identify words that begin with each letter.
  • Build confidence when speaking and reading.

Short story

Ada saw a big red ball near the door. Her teacher asked, “What sound starts the word ball?” Ada smiled and said, “B!” Then she found a bag, a book, and a bottle. She discovered that learning letters can feel like a treasure hunt.

Lesson for today

Letters are the building blocks of words. When children know letters and sounds, reading becomes less frightening.

Children do not need to master everything in one day. Small daily practice works better than pressure.

Practice activity

Choose five letters. For each letter, ask the child to say the letter name, make the sound, and find one object that begins with that sound. Draw the object after naming it.

Think and talk

  • What letter did you enjoy today?
  • What sound was easy to remember?
  • What word can you say that begins with your favorite letter?

Home or classroom task

Create an alphabet corner at home or in class. Add one new letter each day with a drawing or object attached to it.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Use praise and repetition. Do not shame children for forgetting. Literacy grows best when children feel safe and encouraged.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Numbers Fun
description: A practical early numeracy guide that helps children count, compare, sort, and understand numbers using daily objects.
contentHtml:
Numbers Fun

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children see numbers in real life using movement, toys, household objects, food items, and simple games.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Count objects from 1 to 20.
  • Understand more, less, and equal.
  • Match numbers to quantities.
  • Practice patience and focus.

Short story

Tomi had five bottle tops. His sister gave him two more. Tomi counted slowly: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. He learned that numbers can grow when we add more.

Lesson for today

Numbers are not just things children say by memory. A number tells us how many items we have.

Touching and moving objects while counting helps children understand quantity.

Practice activity

Place objects on a table. Ask the child to count them, then add more or remove some. Use phrases like: “How many now?” “Which side has more?” “Are they equal?”

Think and talk

  • What number did you count to today?
  • Which group had more?
  • Where do you see numbers at home, school, or church?

Home or classroom task

Ask the child to count safe objects at home: spoons, shoes, cups, books, fruits, or pencils. Let them draw the number afterward.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Avoid rushing children. Repetition is normal. Encourage effort before accuracy so the child does not become afraid of mathematics.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Colors and Shapes
description: A colorful observation guide that helps children recognize colors, shapes, patterns, and objects in their environment.
contentHtml:
Colors and Shapes

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps children observe the world around them, name colors and shapes, and express ideas through drawing and sorting.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Name common colors.
  • Recognize circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles.
  • Identify shapes in real objects.
  • Create simple patterns.

Short story

Muna looked around her classroom and saw shapes everywhere. The clock was a circle, the door was a rectangle, and her snack box was a square. She realized shapes were hiding in plain sight.

Lesson for today

Colors and shapes help children describe what they see.

Observation builds language, attention, memory, and early problem-solving.

Practice activity

Go on a color and shape hunt. Ask the child to find three blue items, two circles, one square, and one rectangle. Let them point, say the name, and describe each object.

Think and talk

  • What is your favorite color?
  • Which shape was easiest to find?
  • What can you build using shapes?

Home or classroom task

Draw a house using a square, triangle, rectangle, and circle. Color each shape differently and ask the child to explain the picture.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Use ordinary objects. Children do not need expensive learning tools; cups, plates, books, doors, windows, and clothing can teach powerful lessons.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Good Manners
description: A character-building guide that teaches respect, polite words, gratitude, apologies, patience, and responsible behavior.
contentHtml:
Good Manners

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children understand that respect and kindness are daily choices that make home, school, and community life better.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Use polite words correctly.
  • Show respect to adults and peers.
  • Apologize when wrong.
  • Practice patience and turn-taking.

Short story

During lunch, Chika wanted water. He almost shouted, but he remembered his manners and said, “Please, may I have some water?” His friend smiled and passed it to him. Chika replied, “Thank you.” Small words made the moment peaceful.

Lesson for today

Good manners are not weakness. They show self-control and respect.

Words like please, thank you, excuse me, sorry, and you are welcome help people feel valued.

Practice activity

Role-play three scenes: asking for help, interrupting politely, and apologizing after hurting someone. Let children practice the wrong way and the better way.

Think and talk

  • Which polite word do you use often?
  • Which polite word do you need to practice?
  • How do you feel when someone speaks kindly to you?

Home or classroom task

Create a manners chart for one week. Tick each time the child uses a polite word without being forced.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Children copy adults. Model the same manners you expect. Correct calmly and privately where possible.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: My Feelings
description: An emotional wellbeing guide that helps children name feelings, understand body signals, and express emotions safely.
contentHtml:
My Feelings

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children understand that feelings are normal and can be expressed in safe, respectful ways.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Name common feelings.
  • Notice body signals.
  • Talk about emotions without shame.
  • Choose safe actions when feelings are strong.

Short story

Zara felt angry when her pencil broke. She wanted to shout, but her teacher asked, “What is your feeling called?” Zara said, “I feel angry.” Then she took a breath and asked for another pencil.

Lesson for today

Feelings are not bad. They give us information about what is happening inside us.

A child can feel angry, sad, worried, jealous, excited, or scared and still choose a safe action.

Practice activity

Use a feeling thermometer from 1 to 5. Ask the child to rate the feeling, name it, and choose one calming action to move down one step.

Think and talk

  • What feeling did you have today?
  • Where did you feel it in your body?
  • Who can you talk to when feelings are too big?

Home or classroom task

Draw four faces: happy, sad, angry, and worried. Under each face, write or say one thing that can cause that feeling.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Do not dismiss emotions with “stop crying” or “you are fine.” Help the child name the feeling, feel safe, and choose a better action.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Safety First
description: A child protection guide that teaches personal safety, trusted adults, unsafe secrets, boundaries, and help-seeking.
contentHtml:
Safety First

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide teaches children how to protect their body, emotions, and environment while knowing when to speak up and ask for help.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Understand safe and unsafe touch.
  • Identify trusted adults.
  • Reject unsafe secrets.
  • Ask for help clearly and quickly.

Short story

Bola felt uncomfortable when an older child asked her to keep a secret that made her scared. She remembered her safety lesson and told her teacher. The teacher listened and helped her stay safe.

Lesson for today

Your body belongs to you. No one should force unsafe touch or unsafe secrets.

A safe secret makes people happy, like a birthday surprise. An unsafe secret makes a child feel scared, confused, threatened, or ashamed.

Practice activity

Ask the child to draw a safety circle with three trusted adults. Practice saying: “I need help. Something happened and I want to talk.”

Think and talk

  • Who is in your safety circle?
  • What should you do if someone asks you to keep an unsafe secret?
  • Where can you go for help in school?

Home or classroom task

Practice emergency information: full name, caregiver name, phone number if possible, and where to find help in school.

Safety / wellbeing note

If a child reports harm, listen calmly, believe them, protect them, and seek appropriate professional or safeguarding support immediately.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Teach safety calmly, not fearfully. Children must know they will not be blamed for reporting unsafe behavior.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Healthy Habits
description: A wellbeing guide that teaches sleep, food, hygiene, movement, screen balance, and daily self-care routines.
contentHtml:
Healthy Habits

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps children understand how small daily habits support learning, energy, mood, and confidence.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Build simple routines.
  • Understand sleep, food, hygiene, and movement.
  • Practice screen balance.
  • Notice how habits affect feelings.

Short story

Emeka felt tired in class because he slept late. The next day, he slept earlier, drank water, and ate breakfast. He noticed he could listen better and play with more energy.

Lesson for today

Healthy habits do not need to be perfect. Small repeated actions can make the body and mind stronger.

Sleep, food, water, movement, hygiene, and rest all affect how children feel and learn.

Practice activity

Create a healthy day checklist: drank water, moved my body, washed hands, brushed teeth, ate something nourishing, rested, and spoke kindly to myself.

Think and talk

  • Which healthy habit is easy for you?
  • Which habit do you need help with?
  • How does your body feel when you rest well?

Home or classroom task

Choose one habit to practice for seven days. Use a tick chart and celebrate effort at the end of the week.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Avoid body-shaming or fear-based health messages. Teach habits as care, not punishment.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Story Time
description: A reading and reflection guide that helps children learn values, emotions, vocabulary, and problem-solving through stories.
contentHtml:
Story Time

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide uses stories to help children build imagination, vocabulary, empathy, and decision-making skills.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Listen with attention.
  • Retell stories in simple words.
  • Identify characters and lessons.
  • Connect stories to real life.

Short story

Nneka read a story about a child who shared lunch with a new student. After the story, she said, “Maybe I can help someone who feels lonely too.” A story helped her think about kindness.

Lesson for today

Stories allow children to practice life lessons safely.

A good story can teach courage, patience, honesty, kindness, safety, and emotional awareness.

Practice activity

Read a short story. Pause and ask: Who is the main character? What problem happened? How did the character feel? What choice did they make?

Think and talk

  • What did the character learn?
  • What would you have done?
  • How does this story connect to your life?

Home or classroom task

Ask the child to draw one scene from the story and say one lesson from it.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Do not focus only on reading accuracy. Use stories to build confidence, listening, vocabulary, empathy, and moral reasoning.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Reading Club
description: A structured guide for reading groups, vocabulary practice, peer discussion, confidence-building, and respectful participation.
contentHtml:
Reading Club

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps schools and families create reading groups where learners read, discuss, ask questions, and build confidence.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Build a regular reading habit.
  • Discuss books respectfully.
  • Learn new vocabulary.
  • Speak confidently in a group.

Short story

A group of students started reading every Friday. At first, some were shy. After a few weeks, they began explaining stories, asking questions, and helping each other with difficult words.

Lesson for today

A reading club is not a place to laugh at weak readers. It is a place to grow together.

Reading improves language, confidence, imagination, and school performance.

Practice activity

Choose a short text. Read silently for 10 minutes. Let each learner read one paragraph aloud, then discuss three new words and one lesson.

Think and talk

  • What new word did you learn?
  • What part of the reading stood out?
  • How can this lesson help you this week?

Home or classroom task

Create a vocabulary notebook. Each week, write five new words, their meanings, and one sentence for each word.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Protect shy learners. Start with pairs before asking them to read to the whole group. Confidence grows gradually.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Mathematics Fun
description: A math confidence guide that teaches addition, subtraction, comparison, real-life problem-solving, and calm practice.
contentHtml:
Mathematics Fun

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children see mathematics as useful, practical, and less frightening through real objects and everyday examples.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Practice addition and subtraction.
  • Use objects to solve problems.
  • Understand math in daily life.
  • Build confidence with numbers.

Short story

Sade had eight oranges. She gave three to her friends. Instead of guessing, she counted what remained and found five. Math helped her solve a real problem.

Lesson for today

Math is not only for the classroom. It helps with sharing, buying, measuring, cooking, time, and planning.

Using real objects makes abstract numbers easier to understand.

Practice activity

Use beans, stones, bottle tops, or pencils. Create five addition and five subtraction questions. Let the child move the objects while solving.

Think and talk

  • What math question did you solve today?
  • What part was difficult?
  • How can you use math at home or in the market?

Home or classroom task

Ask the child to create three real-life math stories, such as sharing snacks, counting cups, or adding pencils.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Do not label a child as “bad at math.” Anxiety blocks learning. Use patience, practice, and praise for effort.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Science Explorers
description: A curiosity-building science guide that encourages observation, safe experiments, questioning, recording, and explaining evidence.
contentHtml:
Science Explorers

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps learners become curious observers who ask questions, test ideas safely, and explain what they discover.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Ask scientific questions.
  • Observe carefully.
  • Make predictions.
  • Record and explain findings.

Short story

Ibrahim noticed that a leaf floated but a coin sank. He asked, “Why?” His teacher smiled and said, “That question is where science begins.”

Lesson for today

Science is a way of learning about the world using observation and evidence.

Good scientists are not people who know everything. They are people who ask good questions and investigate safely.

Practice activity

Try a floating and sinking experiment with safe items: leaf, spoon, bottle cap, coin, small stick. Predict first, test next, then record what happened.

Think and talk

  • What surprised you?
  • What question do you still have?
  • What did your evidence show?

Home or classroom task

Keep a three-day observation journal of a plant, shadow, cloud, or water container. Write or draw one change each day.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Supervise experiments. Children should not mix unknown chemicals, taste experiment materials, use fire, or handle sharp objects without adult support.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Creative Drawing
description: A creative expression guide that helps children use drawing to communicate ideas, feelings, family stories, and imagination.
contentHtml:
Creative Drawing

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children express thoughts, emotions, imagination, and stories through drawing without fear of being judged.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Use drawing to express ideas.
  • Describe pictures in words.
  • Practice fine motor control.
  • Build confidence through creativity.

Short story

Little Kosi drew a big yellow sun and three people holding hands. When her teacher asked about it, Kosi said, “This is my happy day.” Her drawing helped her speak.

Lesson for today

Drawing is more than art. It can help children communicate feelings before they have all the words.

The goal is not perfection. The goal is expression.

Practice activity

Fold a paper into four boxes. Ask the child to draw: someone I love, something I like, a place I feel safe, and something I want to learn.

Think and talk

  • What is happening in your picture?
  • What feeling does your drawing show?
  • What colors did you choose and why?

Home or classroom task

Create a small art folder. Keep drawings and revisit them later so the child can see progress.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Avoid over-correcting drawings. Praise effort, ideas, color choices, and storytelling.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Public Speaking for Kids
description: A confidence-building speaking guide that teaches children how to organize ideas, speak clearly, and present without shame.
contentHtml:
Public Speaking for Kids

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps learners speak with courage, organize their ideas, and communicate respectfully in front of others.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Prepare a simple speech.
  • Speak clearly and slowly.
  • Manage nervousness.
  • Listen respectfully to others.

Short story

Before presentation day, Musa felt nervous. He practiced with two friends first. When it was his turn, he breathed slowly, greeted the class, and shared three points. He learned that courage grows with practice.

Lesson for today

Public speaking is a skill. Children become better by practicing in safe steps.

A good speech has a greeting, topic, main points, and closing.

Practice activity

Prepare a one-minute speech on one topic: my favorite subject, why kindness matters, my role model, or how to stay safe. Use three clear points.

Think and talk

  • What makes speaking scary?
  • What helps you feel brave?
  • What topic can you speak about confidently?

Home or classroom task

Practice first alone, then with one trusted person, then with a small group before speaking to a larger group.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Do not use public speaking to embarrass children. Build confidence gradually, especially for shy learners.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Leadership for Kids
description: A leadership guide that teaches responsibility, service, honesty, teamwork, problem-solving, and positive influence.
contentHtml:
Leadership for Kids

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children understand leadership as service, responsibility, courage, and doing what is right.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Understand servant leadership.
  • Practice responsibility.
  • Use influence positively.
  • Solve problems with respect.

Short story

When the classroom became noisy, Amara did not shout at everyone. She helped arrange the books, invited others to join, and reminded the group of their task. She led by example.

Lesson for today

Leadership is not controlling people. It is helping people move toward what is good.

A leader listens, tells the truth, protects others, solves problems, and accepts correction.

Practice activity

Choose one leadership challenge for the week: welcome a new student, help clean a space, encourage a classmate, or report unsafe behavior.

Think and talk

  • How can you lead without being proud?
  • What problem can you help solve?
  • Who is a leader you admire and why?

Home or classroom task

Create a leadership diary. Write one responsible action you took each day for five days.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Give children real responsibilities. Leadership grows when children are trusted, guided, and held accountable.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Emotional Intelligence
description: A deeper emotional wellbeing guide that teaches self-awareness, empathy, self-control, choices, and relationship skills.
contentHtml:
Emotional Intelligence

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps learners understand their emotions, manage their actions, and respect how others feel.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Notice and name emotions.
  • Pause before reacting.
  • Show empathy.
  • Repair harm after mistakes.

Short story

David was angry when his teammate blamed him. He wanted to shout, but he paused and said, “I feel upset because I tried my best.” The conversation changed because he used words instead of insults.

Lesson for today

Emotional intelligence means understanding feelings and choosing wise actions.

Feelings and actions are different. You can feel angry and still choose not to hurt someone.

Practice activity

Practice the four-step method: notice the feeling, name the feeling, understand the reason, choose a safe action.

Think and talk

  • What feeling is hardest for you to manage?
  • What helps you calm down?
  • How can you show empathy this week?

Home or classroom task

Write about one moment when you reacted badly. Then write what you could do differently next time.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Help children repair harm, not just receive punishment. Ask: What happened? Who was affected? What can you do to make it better?

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Environmental Awareness
description: A community responsibility guide that teaches cleanliness, care for nature, waste reduction, water care, and environmental leadership.
contentHtml:
Environmental Awareness

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource teaches children that caring for the environment is part of caring for people, animals, plants, and the community.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Understand what the environment is.
  • Practice cleanliness.
  • Care for plants and water.
  • Take responsibility for shared spaces.

Short story

After break time, the school compound was full of wrappers. A group of children picked up the litter and placed it in a bin. The space looked better, and everyone felt proud.

Lesson for today

The environment includes air, water, land, plants, animals, homes, schools, roads, and communities.

A clean environment supports health, safety, dignity, and learning.

Practice activity

Choose one small area such as a desk, classroom corner, or home space. Clean it, arrange it, and discuss how it feels afterward.

Think and talk

  • Why should we keep our school clean?
  • What happens when people throw trash everywhere?
  • What one environmental habit can you practice?

Home or classroom task

Observe one plant for three days. Draw it and write what it needs to grow: water, sunlight, soil, air, and care.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Use environmental care as a leadership lesson. Avoid using cleaning as humiliation; teach it as shared responsibility.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Kind Words
description: A communication and kindness guide that teaches children how words affect feelings, friendship, bullying, and repair.
contentHtml:
Kind Words

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children understand that words can heal, encourage, include, and protect—or hurt, shame, and exclude.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Use encouraging words.
  • Avoid insults and mockery.
  • Repair hurtful speech.
  • Include others kindly.

Short story

During a game, one child made a mistake. Some children laughed, but Naya said, “It is okay. Try again.” Her kind words helped the child feel brave enough to continue.

Lesson for today

Kind words are not small. They can change how someone feels about themselves.

Hurtful words can remain in a person’s heart long after the moment has passed.

Practice activity

Practice replacing hurtful words with kind words. Example: Instead of “You are bad at this,” say “You can try again.”

Think and talk

  • What kind word made you feel good before?
  • Have you ever used words that hurt someone?
  • How can you repair hurtful words?

Home or classroom task

Say one kind sentence to three people today: someone at home, someone in class, and someone who may feel left out.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Correct unkind speech early. Teach children to apologize clearly and change the behavior.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Sharing and Teamwork
description: A social development guide that teaches turn-taking, cooperation, asking politely, helping others, and working together.
contentHtml:
Sharing and Teamwork

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps young children practice patience, cooperation, turn-taking, and respectful play.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Take turns with toys and materials.
  • Ask politely to join.
  • Work with others.
  • Celebrate group success.

Short story

Two children wanted the same toy truck. Their teacher gave them a timer. One child played first, then passed it to the other. They learned that taking turns can be fair.

Lesson for today

Sharing does not always mean giving everything away. It means learning fairness, patience, and kindness.

Teamwork means working together so everyone contributes.

Practice activity

Give children blocks or paper and ask them to build something together. Assign simple roles: builder, helper, counter, and speaker.

Think and talk

  • How do you feel when someone shares with you?
  • How can you ask for a turn kindly?
  • What can your team do better next time?

Home or classroom task

Practice phrases: “Can I have a turn?” “You can use it after me.” “Let us do it together.” “Thank you for sharing.”

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Young children are still learning impulse control. Use timers, clear rules, calm reminders, and praise for cooperative behavior.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: My Safety Circle
description: A practical safety guide that helps children identify trusted adults and know what to do when they feel unsafe or overwhelmed.
contentHtml:
My Safety Circle

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This resource helps every child identify trusted adults they can speak to when they feel worried, confused, unsafe, or hurt.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Name trusted adults.
  • Know when to ask for help.
  • Practice reporting unsafe situations.
  • Keep seeking help until someone listens.

Short story

Grace felt scared after being bullied. She first told a friend, but the bullying continued. Then she told her teacher and aunt. Her safety circle helped stop the problem.

Lesson for today

A safety circle is made up of people who listen, protect, guide, and act responsibly.

If the first adult does not listen, a child should tell another trusted adult.

Practice activity

Draw a hand. On each finger, write one trusted adult. Practice saying: “I need help. Something happened and I want to talk.”

Think and talk

  • Who listens to you well?
  • Who helps you feel safe?
  • What should you do if the first adult does not listen?

Home or classroom task

Place the safety circle drawing somewhere safe. Review it monthly and update names if needed.

Safety / wellbeing note

If a child reports abuse, harm, threats, or self-harm thoughts, get immediate safeguarding or professional support.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Children should never be punished for speaking up about safety. Adults must listen calmly and take action.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.

title: Calm Down Toolbox
description: An emotional regulation guide that teaches breathing, grounding, naming feelings, safe support, and coping during overwhelm.
contentHtml:
Calm Down Toolbox

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide gives learners practical tools to use when anger, worry, embarrassment, fear, or sadness feels too strong.

What this guide helps children learn

  • Pause before reacting.
  • Use breathing and grounding.
  • Name feelings clearly.
  • Ask for safe support.

Short story

During a disagreement, Tola felt his chest tighten and his face grow hot. Instead of shouting, he stepped back, breathed slowly, and said, “I need a minute.” His calm-down toolbox helped him choose safety.

Lesson for today

Strong feelings are normal, but unsafe reactions can create bigger problems.

A calm-down toolbox gives the brain and body time to settle before making a choice.

Practice activity

Practice 5-4-3-2-1 grounding: name 5 things you see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you hear, 2 things you smell, and 1 safe thing you can do next.

Think and talk

  • What feeling do you need help calming?
  • Which tool works best for you?
  • Who can you talk to when you are overwhelmed?

Home or classroom task

Create a personal toolbox list: breathing, prayer or quiet reflection, drawing, talking to a trusted adult, walking away safely, drinking water, or writing feelings down.

Safety / wellbeing note

If a young person feels like harming themselves or someone else, they should tell a trusted adult immediately and receive urgent support.

For parents, teachers and facilitators

Teach coping skills before a crisis. Children remember tools better when they practice while calm.

My SpeakOut promise

I will learn with confidence, ask for help when I need it, treat others with kindness, and take one safe step every day.
